body.content:
Hi Erkki, I'm at the site now. Changed the SFP on transmission node TRN-042.
Link is up and alarms cleared, but traffic is still not coming back. Have you seen this before?
Yes. Is this one of the older units?
Yes, installed around 2019 I think.

Ok. Don't trust the green link status on those.
Sometimes after changing the SFP the interface comes up normally, but the forwarding state doesn't recover correctly.
So another SFP?

No. Usually the SFP is fine.
Check whether the traffic counters are actually increasing. If they stay at zero even though the interface is UP, it's probably the issue I've seen before.
Yes. Link UP. RX power looks normal. Counters basically zero.

That's it.
Disable the interface, wait a little, then enable it again. Don't reboot the whole unit unless that fails.
Did that. Traffic is back 👍
Good. These old units sometimes behave like this after an optical module replacement.
Is this documented somewhere?

Not that I know of 😄
We've just learned it over the years.

FYI: the disable/enable workaround for the older transmission units is no longer needed after firmware 4.2.
The fix removes the stuck forwarding state after an optical module replacement.
Good to know, thanks 👍
Lunch at 12?
Ok 👍
Hi Olli, I'm looking into an issue at the Tampere site. Some devices lost connectivity after the primary gateway restarted. The gateway is back online, but a few devices are still unreachable.
Interesting. Are all devices affected, or only some of them?
Only some. The majority recovered automatically. The affected devices can reach their local switches, but communication with other subnets fails.
That sounds familiar. We had almost the same symptoms in ticket INC-1938 last year. It was caused by outdated ARP entries after a gateway failover.
I haven't worked with that before. I thought ARP entries would update automatically when the gateway changed.
Normally they do, but older devices don't always handle these updates correctly. Some keep the previous IP-to-MAC mapping until the entry expires or is refreshed.
So the devices might still be sending traffic to the old gateway MAC address even though the primary gateway is active again?

Exactly. First, compare the gateway MAC address in the affected devices' ARP tables with the MAC address currently advertised by the active gateway. Don't clear anything yet. Let's confirm the mismatch before changing the state.
I checked two affected devices. Both have the previous MAC address cached. The gateway is advertising a different one now.
Good find. That matches the previous incident. In INC-1938, we found that the legacy gateway wasn't consistently sending gratuitous ARP announcements after recovering from failover.
Is that something we can fix without restarting the gateway?

Yes, potentially. Follow the approved procedure for refreshing the affected ARP entries on the relevant devices, rather than flushing the entire network's ARP tables. We should also review the gateway's failover configuration and announcement settings.
Understood. I'll collect the current ARP entries and compare them with the gateway information before making any changes.
We refreshed the affected entries following the maintenance procedure. Connectivity is restored on both devices, and traffic looks normal again.
Excellent. Please document the findings and link INC-1938 to the new incident. It will help the next person who encounters this behaviour.
Will do. Thanks for the help! I wouldn't have thought to check the ARP cache since the gateway itself looked healthy.
That's why it's worth looking beyond interface status and alarms. The network can look perfectly healthy while individual devices are still using outdated information 😄
Has anyone checked SW-208? We're getting intermittent packet loss between the access network and the distribution layer.
I checked it this morning. The switch is pretty old, so I suspect a hardware issue. We've had similar problems with that model before.
I don't think we should blame the hardware yet. CPU usage is normal, interfaces are stable, and there are no hardware alarms.
That doesn't mean the switch is healthy. These older models can have forwarding problems without reporting any obvious alarms.
Maybe, but replacing a distribution switch because of packet loss without checking the configuration first seems a bit premature.
We've already checked the uplink. No CRC errors, no speed mismatch, and optical levels are fine. What else do you want to check?
The VLAN configuration. I noticed someone changed the allowed VLAN list on the uplink yesterday. Could be related.
That was part of a separate maintenance task. It shouldn't affect the other VLANs.
It might if the configuration was applied incorrectly. The change log shows VLAN 340 was removed from the allowed list.
Wait, VLAN 340 is used by the monitoring servers. But why would that cause packet loss on other devices?
You're both making reasonable points, but let's separate the symptoms. Are the affected devices all using VLAN 340, or are completely unrelated VLANs also experiencing packet loss?
I checked the affected endpoints. Most of them are in VLAN 340. The others seem to have normal connectivity.
Okay, that changes things. I assumed the packet loss was happening across the entire switch.

This is why we shouldn't jump to hardware replacement. The switch is a legacy model, but that doesn't automatically make it responsible. We need to verify the maintenance change against the approved configuration.
I compared the current configuration with the backup from last week. VLAN 340 was definitely present before the maintenance.
Found the change request. The engineer updated the allowed VLAN list but used an incomplete list from an older configuration template. Looks like VLAN 340 was accidentally omitted.
So it wasn't the switch after all 😄
Not this time. I still think we should plan a replacement eventually, though. That firmware is getting quite old.

Agreed on the replacement plan, but let's handle the immediate issue first. Restore the approved VLAN configuration through the change procedure, verify connectivity, and monitor the interface counters afterward.
Configuration restored. VLAN 340 is passing traffic again. Packet loss has stopped in the monitoring dashboard.
Good catch, Mikko. I was too quick to blame the hardware. I'll add the missing VLAN to the maintenance checklist so we don't repeat this.
Good outcome. Let's document the root cause and link the configuration change to the incident. And remember: experience is useful, but evidence should win the argument 😉
Hi Riku, I've got a strange issue with workstation WS-314. The user says internal applications aren't opening, but internet access works normally.
Are they getting any error messages, or do the applications just keep loading?
Mostly DNS errors. They can open public websites, but internal server names don't resolve.
Sounds like DNS. Did you check whether the workstation received the correct DNS server address from DHCP?
Not yet. I was going to restart the switch port because I thought it might be a connectivity issue.
I'd hold off on that. If internet access works and the user has a valid IP address, the switch is probably doing its job. Let's check DNS first.
Just checked the network settings. The DNS server address is different from the one assigned to other workstations in the same subnet.
There we go. It might have been manually configured at some point. Check whether the adapter is supposed to obtain DNS settings automatically.
It should use DHCP. Someone must have entered the old DNS address manually.
That would explain it. Restore the approved automatic DNS configuration, renew the DHCP settings, and test an internal hostname again.
Done. The workstation received the correct DNS servers, and the internal applications are opening now.
Perfect. No switch restart or network changes needed after all 😄
Definitely an easier fix than I expected. I'll add the incorrect DNS configuration to the ticket notes.
Good idea. Always worth checking the basics before troubleshooting the entire network!
Hey, I think I might have broken something on SW-104. I was cleaning up the VLAN configuration and now a few people in the office have lost network access.
Okay, first of all, don't make any more changes 😄 What exactly did you modify?
I removed what I thought were unused VLANs from the switch. The ports are still UP, but devices in one office area can't reach the internal servers.
Did you remove VLANs from the database or change the allowed VLAN list on the uplink?
The allowed VLAN list. I thought the VLANs that weren't being used locally could be removed.
Oh no. That uplink carries traffic for several other switches. A VLAN can be needed on the trunk even if there aren't any devices using it directly on this switch.
I didn't realise that. I removed VLAN 120 and VLAN 180 because I couldn't find any active devices assigned to them.

That explains the symptoms. VLAN 120 is used by the office workstations, and VLAN 180 carries some internal services. They need to pass through this switch even though their endpoints are connected elsewhere.
Can I just add them back to the list?

Yes, but first let's compare the current configuration with the last approved backup. We need to make sure nothing else was accidentally removed. We'll restore the missing entries through the normal change procedure.
I've checked the configuration backup. Those are the only two missing VLANs from the trunk. Everything else matches.
The approved configuration has been restored with Antti supervising. Should we test the affected workstations now?
Yes. Check connectivity to the internal servers first, then verify that the monitoring system shows normal traffic on both VLANs.
Everything is working again. Both VLANs are passing traffic and the users have connectivity.
Good. I've updated the incident with the configuration backup and the details of what happened.
Sorry about that. I honestly thought I was just removing unused configuration.

Don't worry, these things happen. But remember that network devices often forward traffic for other parts of the network. Just because you don't see a local device using a VLAN doesn't mean it's unnecessary.
Lesson learned. I'll definitely check the topology and configuration backup before touching trunk settings next time.
That's the right attitude. And next time, ask before cleaning up production switches 😂
Morning. We've got another connectivity issue at the Helsinki office. The application servers are reachable from the local network, but connections from the remote sites are timing out.
Didn't we have something similar last month? I remember working on a firewall issue for the same server subnet.
Yes, ticket INC-3264. But that one was related to a routing issue. The routes look correct this time.
I found something in the change history. There was a firewall policy update yesterday evening, linked to request CHG-1842.
Interesting. Was that the change requested by the application team? I remember receiving an email about opening a new connection for their monitoring service.
I found the email. It was sent by Thomas from the application team on Tuesday. The subject was 'Firewall access required for monitoring migration'.
Can you check whether the request included only the new monitoring connection or whether they asked to modify the existing rules as well?
Just checked. The email specifically says that existing remote-site access should remain unchanged. But the change notes mention that an older firewall group was replaced.
That's not good. Could the replacement group be missing the remote-site subnet objects?
Possibly. I compared the current policy with the configuration from INC-3264. Two remote-site networks are missing from the source group.
Before we conclude anything, check the original change request and its approval comments. We need to establish whether those networks were intentionally excluded or simply overlooked.
The approval comments don't mention removing any existing access. It looks like the new group was created from an outdated spreadsheet attached to the email.
So we basically copied an old network list and replaced the existing group without checking all its members?
That's what it looks like. I also found an email from the remote-site team sent after the change. They reported connection failures, but it was attached to a different service ticket.
Which ticket? We should probably link that to the current incident.
SR-7712. It was originally categorized as an application issue, so nobody connected it to the firewall maintenance.

Okay, now we have a likely explanation. Let's document the relationship between INC-3264, CHG-1842 and SR-7712. Once the approved source networks have been confirmed with the application team, we can correct the firewall group through the change procedure.
I've emailed Thomas to confirm the two missing subnets. He replied that both should definitely retain access. The spreadsheet was an old version.
The approved correction has been applied. I've tested connectivity from both remote sites, and the application servers are responding again.
Great. I'll update the incident and attach the email confirmation from Thomas so there's a clear record of the requested access.

Good work. Please also add a note to CHG-1842 explaining that the outdated spreadsheet caused existing network entries to be omitted. We should avoid closing the original change without documenting that.
Will do. Quite a lot of detective work for two missing network entries 😄
That's infrastructure work sometimes. The actual fix can take five minutes. Finding out why it happened can take half a day.
